relevance.rationale: A shared website integration delivered code across customer trust boundaries; relevant to teams embedding third-party scripts.

detail.rationale: The updated report connects a signup-flow vulnerability, modified customer JavaScript and browser-side payloads, but does not publish a complete exploit or victim-loss accounting.

transferability.rationale: Supports concrete review of publishing authority, script inventory, emergency distribution shutdown and browser-side data boundaries.

confidence.rationale: Vendor statements and researcher findings are attributed through secondary reporting; file counts and payload capability do not establish realized theft for every customer.

report:b6e25351df538f83532c.why: This is a distribution-trust failure, not merely another malicious website: an integration already trusted by customer pages became the delivery channel.
report:b6e25351df538f83532c.learn: Trace who can change each externally loaded script. Design a way to suspend compromised distribution without waiting for every customer to deploy; distinguish an attacker's payload capability from proven data loss.

diagram.normal: Customer websites load Optimizely-managed JavaScript to run their configured experiments and integrations.
diagram.root_cause: The report attributes unauthorized project changes to a vulnerability in Optimizely's signup flow; the trusted script channel then distributed attacker-modified JavaScript.
diagram.contributors: Customer browsers already trusted the integration. A control-plane compromise therefore crossed into many independent customer pages.
diagram.symptoms: Researchers found scripts with wallet replacement, card-skimming and mobile-payload behavior. Observed file counts are not counts of visitors whose data was stolen.

steps.label: Customer loads trusted integration
steps.detail: A customer page includes vendor-managed JavaScript, so changes to that code can execute in the customer's browser context.

steps.label: Signup-flow weakness abused
steps.detail: The updated report attributes access to customer projects to a vulnerability in the signup flow; it does not provide a complete exploit reconstruction.

steps.label: Project scripts modified
steps.detail: Malicious JavaScript was inserted into customer projects and delivered through the existing trusted integration.

steps.label: Browser-side payload exposure
steps.detail: Reported payloads could replace wallet addresses, collect payment-form inputs or deliver an iOS payload. Capability does not prove each visitor suffered theft.

steps.label: Distribution and access contained
steps.detail: The company reported blocking the path, removing malicious code and ending or resetting affected access. These controls limit propagation; they do not establish what happened before containment.

relevance.rationale: An obsolete vendor credential became an entry point into connected cloud systems; common across integration-heavy software estates.

detail.rationale: The report describes credential origin, subsequent service access and an attempted persistence path, but leaves uncertainty about actual integration-secret access.

transferability.rationale: Credential retirement, privilege boundaries and cross-service compromise mapping provide several specific controls and useful tradeoffs.

confidence.rationale: Detailed vendor claims are conveyed through a secondary article. AI-tool attribution and absence-of-access claims remain attributed assessments.

report:ac17c0218f3e057f3e39.why: The useful failure is the lifetime and reach of a leftover access key. An AI-related attack label is not necessary to understand that control failure.
report:ac17c0218f3e057f3e39.learn: Make project closure retire credentials, not just infrastructure. Review whether one integration identity can discover credentials for the next service, and practice revocation across that dependency chain.

diagram.normal: A vendor-issued key should authorize only the active integration for which it was created.
diagram.root_cause: According to the report, a stolen vendor cloud key remained valid after its project ended. How it was initially stolen is described as the company's belief, not independently established.
diagram.contributors: Reachable analytics, source and Kubernetes systems created opportunities for credential chaining after entry.
diagram.symptoms: Unauthorized cross-service activity and an attempted container-based persistence path were detected; the report does not establish theft of all reachable integration credentials.

steps.label: Vendor integration uses a key
steps.detail: A cloud access key originally served a vendor project. Authorization should have ended with that project's need.

steps.label: Old key remains usable
steps.detail: The company says attackers used a vendor key that had not been retired; it believed the credential was stolen from the vendor.

steps.label: Access chains across services
steps.detail: The account describes movement through analytics, source and Kubernetes systems, illustrating why reachable secret stores enlarge blast radius.

steps.label: Sensitive systems reached
steps.detail: An integration-credential system was reached, but the vendor said it had no evidence its stored credentials were accessed or stolen. Reachability and confirmed theft differ.

steps.label: Contain and rotate credentials
steps.detail: The account reports blocked activity and precautionary credential rotation. Rotation responds to uncertain exposure; it does not prove every rotated secret was stolen.

report:91e784d7cca7318ca4d6.model: Copilot incident-writer (inherited model unexposed); parent review gpt-6.1-sol

relevance.rationale: Shared gateway overload and cascading failover are directly useful to operators of replicated services.

detail.rationale: A concrete feedback loop, concurrent capacity reduction and representative-test gap are described, but the public account quotes a preliminary nonpublic Microsoft report.

transferability.rationale: Connects load shedding, spare capacity, realistic high-core testing and backlog-aware recovery rather than recommending more capacity alone.

confidence.rationale: The mechanism is attributed to Microsoft's preliminary report via BleepingComputer; it is not independently reproduced or supported by a public final postmortem.

report:91e784d7cca7318ca4d6.why: BleepingComputer's preliminary account gives a concrete counterexample to redundancy as automatic isolation: redistribution can concentrate the same stress on the capacity needed for recovery. It supports a feedback-loop analysis without requiring an invented gateway topology.
report:91e784d7cca7318ca4d6.learn: Use the architecture exercise to identify a stable operating envelope during combined traffic transfer and capacity loss, then test whether the same envelope allows backlog to drain during recovery.

diagram.normal: BleepingComputer-based assessment: a shared gateway layer serves multiple Microsoft 365 workloads and redirects traffic when gateways become unavailable. Detailed routing topology is not established.
diagram.root_cause: Microsoft's preliminary account via BleepingComputer identifies a latent contention defect activated under changed load and capacity conditions. Neither server count alone nor the latest deployment explains the failure.
diagram.contributors: BleepingComputer-based review: Teams failover added traffic while approximately 14% of capacity was independently offline. Higher-core behavior and unrepresentative laboratory conditions mattered.
diagram.symptoms: BleepingComputer reports gateway unresponsiveness and worldwide disruption. The existing review describes redirected traffic causing further failures; this amplification is distinct from the original defect.

steps.label: Gateways share request load
steps.detail: The BleepingComputer-based assessment describes shared gateways and traffic redirection. This provides continuity only while remaining gateways can process the work they receive; no particular routing algorithm is established.

steps.label: Extra traffic meets less capacity
steps.detail: Microsoft's preliminary account via BleepingComputer combines Teams-failover traffic with independently unavailable capacity. More arriving work and fewer available gateways increase pressure together; the source does not establish a precise threshold.

steps.label: Latent contention stalls gateways
steps.detail: The preliminary account reported by BleepingComputer identifies a months-old contention defect, exacerbated on higher-core hardware. Under the incident conditions, gateways became unresponsive instead of delivering the expected capacity; the exact locking or scheduling mechanism is unpublished here.

steps.label: Survivors inherit more traffic
steps.detail: The BleepingComputer-based review describes traffic redirected from unavailable gateways onto survivors. This transfers demand without restoring processing capacity, so survivors face greater pressure and may also fail. Multiple services were disrupted; regional safeguards did not contain the cascade.

steps.label: Fix, capacity and backlog control
steps.detail: The existing BleepingComputer-based review records a fix, capacity and redirection safeguards, and alternative infrastructure for some services. Restarted processes alone faced overwhelming backlog: restoration had to change the operating condition, not merely revive instances. Detailed sequencing and thresholds are unavailable.

feedback.label: BleepingComputer-based review: redirected demand raises pressure on survivors; further unresponsiveness removes capacity and repeats the overload.

architecture.invariant: Inferred design question: can the gateway layer keep accepted work within surviving effective capacity during simultaneous failover, maintenance loss and recovery? Microsoft's preliminary account via BleepingComputer supports this question, not a claim about an undocumented Microsoft service-level invariant.
architecture.response: Detection: the supplied BleepingComputer-based evidence describes unresponsive gateways but not the initial alert or detection latency. Containment: the review records redirection safeguards and alternative infrastructure, without a complete chronology. Recovery: a software fix and capacity measures addressed conditions that restarts alone did not; backlog was material. Proposed prevention: constrain transfer and admission, validate representative concurrency, and stage recovery as below. No absent vendor control is inferred.

decisions.title: Budget failover against degraded effective capacity
decisions.proposal: Proposed for steps 2 to 3: gate discretionary capacity removal and traffic transfer on an experimentally established safe envelope for the production-like request mix. Hold reserve or defer maintenance when transferred demand would exceed that envelope, reducing entry into the defect-sensitive operating region.
decisions.tradeoff: Reserve costs money; deferred maintenance increases operational risk, and safety margins can unnecessarily restrict otherwise usable capacity.
decisions.residual_risk: A software defect can collapse throughput below the measured envelope. Reserve is not a substitute for remediation or evidence about the contention threshold.

decisions.title: Bound the redirection feedback loop
decisions.proposal: Proposed for the steps 4 to 3 feedback edge: cap transferred admissions per destination and reject or defer excess work before it enters the contended path. Pair this with bounded caller retries so protecting survivors does not regenerate the rejected demand.
decisions.tradeoff: Deliberate rejection sacrifices some requests to preserve useful throughput. Deferral consumes queue capacity and may outlive user deadlines.
decisions.residual_risk: Uncoordinated retries or an inaccurate capacity estimate can still overload survivors. Policy requires workload priorities and client semantics that this evidence does not provide.

decisions.title: Reintroduce capacity with a bounded backlog drain
decisions.proposal: Proposed for steps 4 to 5: place repaired instances behind a gradual admission ramp, reserving a measured completion budget for backlog alongside fresh work. Advance only while useful completions remain stable and queue age falls, preventing restart from recreating the overload.
decisions.tradeoff: Conservative ramps prolong recovery; prioritizing fresh work can starve queued work, while aggressive draining can harm live traffic.
decisions.residual_risk: An unfixed defect can recur at low load; health probes may not represent customer work. Expired or non-idempotent queued operations need separate handling.

architecture.validation: Proposed controlled exercise: on production-representative core counts and concurrency, replay a synthetic workload mix while independently reducing gateway capacity and transferring traffic. Compare unrestricted redirection with capped transfer and admission, then restore one instance under backlog using immediate versus staged admission. Observe useful completions, rejection rate, queue age, contention signals and repeated unresponsiveness. A successful policy keeps failures from spreading and drains backlog without another collapse; process restart alone is not success. Establish workload deadlines, retry behavior, effective throughput and contention traces before selecting limits; no Microsoft threshold is inferred.
architecture.open_questions: Needed evidence: a public final postmortem, the defect and high-core contention mechanism, production/test workload differences, routing and regional dependency boundaries, capacity-loss cause, retry/backlog behavior, and measured effects of each remediation. These determine whether admission, reserve or recovery policy offers the strongest leverage.

relevance.rationale: Browser-side payment collection is directly relevant to commerce teams, though narrower than a shared infrastructure failure.

detail.rationale: The collection surface, affected data and response are described, but the original checkout compromise mechanism and complete victim scope are not established.

transferability.rationale: Supports concrete separation of live form inputs from stored records, script-change monitoring and incident-window review.

confidence.rationale: The account cites the company's notification through secondary reporting; no public technical postmortem establishes initial access.

report:0d946a07bc289f653805.why: It distinguishes payment data stolen as a user types from theft of an existing backend database; those paths require different controls.
report:0d946a07bc289f653805.learn: Map every script that can read payment-form inputs, then test detection and shutdown of an unauthorized checkout change. An unknown initial access path must stay unknown even when the collection mechanism is clear.

diagram.normal: A customer submits payment details through the checkout page to purchase tickets.
diagram.root_cause: The account establishes malicious checkout-page collection, but not how attackers first gained the ability to alter that checkout.
diagram.contributors: Sensitive values entered into a live form were exposed to the compromised page path; that is distinct from a claim that the stored customer database was stolen.
diagram.symptoms: Reported exposure included card details and related checkout fields during October 8-11. The later publication date is not the attack date.

steps.label: Customer enters checkout data
steps.detail: The normal purchase flow accepts payment and associated checkout details.

steps.label: Initial compromise not published
steps.detail: The available account does not explain the initial intrusion or unauthorized change path. No specific exploit is inferred.

steps.label: Checkout skimmer collects input
steps.detail: Fandango's notification, as reported, describes malicious code collecting submitted checkout data during October 8-11.

steps.label: Payment information exposed
steps.detail: Reported fields included card number, expiry, CVV, billing ZIP and email. The company did not report exposure of names, Social Security numbers or account information.

steps.label: Checkout fixed; investigation opened
steps.detail: The company reported fixing the checkout issue and engaging outside investigators. No known fraud is not proof that no misuse will occur.

relevance.rationale: Compromised collaboration identities and developer endpoints are relevant to software organizations, although this is a campaign report rather than one service postmortem.

detail.rationale: The social-engineering-to-endpoint-to-next-contact progression is described; one complete victim environment and recovery timeline are not.

transferability.rationale: Supports independent contact verification, software-installation boundaries and treating a trusted account as potentially compromised.

confidence.rationale: The report attributes the campaign to agencies through secondary reporting; attribution and aggregate losses are not independently validated here.

report:d32b5f97fc676bf8272f.why: A familiar account and a convincing video are identity signals, not authorization to install a supposed meeting repair tool.
report:d32b5f97fc676bf8272f.learn: Model the handoff from social trust to endpoint execution. Practice verifying unusual installation requests through an independent channel, and include contact-account compromise in response planning.

diagram.normal: People use an existing contact and a video call to arrange legitimate professional conversations.
diagram.root_cause: The reported campaign abuses compromised trusted-contact accounts and a fabricated meeting problem to persuade targets to run malicious software.
diagram.contributors: A familiar identity and prerecorded or deepfake video reduced suspicion. These cues do not cryptographically authenticate the requested action.
diagram.symptoms: Endpoint credential theft enabled financial theft and further approaches to the victim's contacts. This is a multi-victim campaign, not one newly dated breach.

steps.label: Conversation with a known contact
steps.detail: The campaign used existing contact relationships as the entry point to professional conversations.

steps.label: Contact account is compromised
steps.detail: An attacker-controlled trusted account invited a target into a staged video interaction.

steps.label: Fake repair crosses execution boundary
steps.detail: A claimed audio problem prompted a malicious software-installation request. The meaningful trust crossing is executing that request, not the video format alone.

steps.label: Endpoint secrets and contacts exposed
steps.detail: The report connects endpoint compromise to stolen credentials, cryptocurrency theft and additional contact targeting. Aggregate losses are agency-attributed claims.

steps.label: Independent verification and response
steps.detail: As a transferable recommendation, verify unusual requests outside the suspect channel; if execution occurred, isolate and investigate the endpoint and revoke affected sessions and secrets. This is advice, not a reported universal victim recovery.

relevance.rationale: Database failover, application locality and consistency-preserving recovery are broadly applicable to stateful services.

detail.rationale: The primary postmortem explains the short partition, quorum decision, divergent writes, restore decision and backlog recovery.

transferability.rationale: Readers can test topology assumptions, failback preconditions and data-integrity tradeoffs rather than assuming a healthy new primary means a healthy application.

confidence.rationale: A detailed first-party retrospective supports the causal sequence and explicitly discusses recovery constraints.

case-github-2018.why: A 43-second network partition produced a much longer service incident because correct database-level failover conflicted with application and data-recovery assumptions.
case-github-2018.learn: Evaluate failover as an application transition, not just a database election. Specify when automatic failback is unsafe and how you reconcile divergent state before replaying queued work.

diagram.normal: Applications and database topology normally relied on local connectivity and established replication relationships.
diagram.root_cause: A network partition triggered a cross-region database promotion. Divergent writes and application locality assumptions made immediate return unsafe or ineffective.
diagram.contributors: Quorum placement favored the western site, while application traffic retained assumptions about the previous database location. Recovery had to preserve data integrity.
diagram.symptoms: Cross-region latency and unavailable or delayed operations persisted after the short partition ended; queued work extended the recovery.

steps.label: Application and databases aligned
steps.detail: The previous placement and replication topology supported the applications' normal latency and availability assumptions.

steps.label: 43-second network partition
steps.detail: The postmortem reports a brief connectivity interruption between facilities during network maintenance.

steps.label: Promotion creates divergent state
steps.detail: Orchestrator promoted western primaries; writes on different sides of the partition meant an immediate failback could lose data.

steps.label: Application locality assumptions fail
steps.detail: Database relocation exposed unacceptable cross-country latency and service degradation. Reconnecting the network did not reconcile divergent databases.

steps.label: Restore, synchronize, process backlog
steps.detail: Responders prioritized integrity, restored and synchronized data, and then processed accumulated work rather than forcing an unsafe fast failback.

relevance.rationale: Configuration-as-code, globally shared request paths and control-plane dependencies apply to many production systems.

detail.rationale: The primary postmortem connects a specific WAF regex performance failure, global delivery path, CPU exhaustion and operational recovery.

transferability.rationale: Provides concrete reasoning for performance budgets, canarying rules, linear-time matching and an emergency control path outside the failing dependency.

confidence.rationale: A detailed first-party retrospective explains the mechanism, limitations of testing and corrective changes.

case-cloudflare-2019.why: A rule in simulate mode still consumed production CPU. Non-blocking business logic can therefore be fully capable of taking down the request path.
case-cloudflare-2019.learn: Treat frequently changed rules as production programs. Test worst-case execution cost, stage their rollout and make the emergency disable mechanism usable during request-path failure.

diagram.normal: The WAF evaluates rules while processing HTTP requests; simulate mode changes enforcement, not the need to execute matching.
diagram.root_cause: A newly deployed regular expression exhibited excessive backtracking and exhausted request-processing CPU.
diagram.contributors: The rule distribution path delivered globally without the staged rollout used for regular software. Some operational access depended on the impaired service.
diagram.symptoms: CPU saturation caused widespread HTTP 502 errors; simulate mode did not prevent resource exhaustion.

steps.label: WAF evaluates incoming requests
steps.detail: Rules run on production traffic even when their enforcement is set to simulate.

steps.label: New rule distributed globally
steps.detail: The WAF rule update followed a global deployment path rather than a staged software-style canary rollout.

steps.label: Regex backtracking exhausts CPU
steps.detail: An inefficient expression consumed available processing resources. This computational mechanism, not a malicious traffic claim, explains the failure.

steps.label: Request processing returns errors
steps.detail: Resource exhaustion produced widespread 502 responses, while shared operational dependencies complicated responder access.

steps.label: Disable WAF; retest before restoring
steps.detail: Responders disabled the WAF globally, removed the problematic rule and re-enabled service after controlled checks.

relevance.rationale: Backup access, privileged human endpoints and linked intrusions are relevant to teams protecting sensitive customer data.

detail.rationale: The retrospective connects two intrusions, endpoint compromise, backup credentials and stolen backup contents, while withholding some forensic detail.

transferability.rationale: Supports threat-modeling restore access, minimizing exported metadata and separating human workstations from high-value backup credentials.

confidence.rationale: A first-party retrospective is substantive but remains the affected company's account, with limits on independently verified exposure and downstream decryption.

case-lastpass-2022.why: Backups are another production data store. Encrypting vault contents did not make their surrounding metadata or the credentials used to reach backups harmless.
case-lastpass-2022.learn: Enumerate the identities, endpoints and secrets that can restore backups. Distinguish stolen ciphertext, unencrypted metadata and proven decryption rather than collapsing them into a single breach claim.

diagram.normal: Backups support recovery of customer data and require tightly controlled access to storage and decryption-related secrets.
diagram.root_cause: The company's account describes linked intrusions culminating in compromise of a DevOps engineer and access to cloud backup storage.
diagram.contributors: Information from the first incident supported targeting in the second; vulnerable third-party software on a privileged human endpoint created another trust boundary.
diagram.symptoms: Backups containing encrypted vault data and unencrypted metadata were stolen. The account does not establish that every vault was decrypted.

steps.label: Backups retain sensitive data
steps.detail: The recovery system stored data whose confidentiality still mattered outside the live service, including encrypted vaults and some unencrypted metadata.

steps.label: First intrusion exposes internal knowledge
steps.detail: The retrospective links the earlier development-environment intrusion to information later used in a separate targeted intrusion.

steps.label: Privileged endpoint compromised
steps.detail: A DevOps engineer was targeted through vulnerable third-party software; the account connects that compromise to credentials and secrets needed for backup access.

steps.label: Cloud backups copied
steps.detail: The attacker obtained backup material containing encrypted vault contents and unencrypted metadata. Stolen encrypted data is not evidence that all plaintext was recovered.

steps.label: Access rebuilt and credentials rotated
steps.detail: The company reported containment and hardening actions and issued customer recommendations. Those actions reduce future access; they cannot recall data already copied.

relevance.rationale: Pull-request availability matters to software delivery teams.

detail.rationale: The retained notices establish degradation, mitigation, monitoring and resolution, but not the failing component or mechanism.

transferability.rationale: Only general incident-communication and workflow-continuity questions are supported; specific prevention controls cannot be inferred.

confidence.rationale: The provider's own status notices support the observed sequence, not a root-cause claim.

github:1xzmt89vv61l.why: Useful as an operational notice, but not yet a strong technical learning case: the retained provider evidence lacks a causal explanation.
github:1xzmt89vv61l.learn: Separate the observed reporting sequence from technical causation. Wait for the promised root-cause account before recommending a particular architectural fix.

diagram.normal: Pull-request workflows normally remain available to contributors.
diagram.root_cause: Cause not published in the retained provider notices.
diagram.contributors: No contributing factors are established by the available status updates.
diagram.symptoms: Pull-request degradation followed by mitigation, monitoring and resolution notices.

steps.label: Pull-request workflow available
steps.detail: This is the affected product's normal user function, not an inferred internal topology.

steps.label: Cause not published
steps.detail: The status evidence does not explain what initiated the degradation. The missing link is intentionally visible.

steps.label: Degradation reported
steps.detail: The provider reported degraded pull-request performance on November 13; reporting timestamps are not a measured outage duration.

steps.label: Mitigated, monitored, resolved
steps.detail: The provider's sequence reports mitigation, monitoring and resolution without identifying the corrective technical change.

relevance.rationale: Actions, Pages and Copilot availability can affect software-development and publication workflows.

detail.rationale: The notices mention recovery and backlog processing but do not identify the original failure mechanism.

transferability.rationale: Backlog verification is a useful recovery question, but the record does not support a technical prevention case study.

confidence.rationale: These are attributed first-party status observations; causal attribution is not available.

github:dvy0t3mvh1lg.why: The distinction between service recovery and backlog completion is useful, but a multi-product impact list alone does not make this a detailed postmortem.
github:dvy0t3mvh1lg.learn: When reviewing recovery, ask whether queued work has finished rather than relying only on a green status. Do not infer a shared database or network cause from simultaneous symptoms.

diagram.normal: The affected products normally serve requests and process queued workflow or publication work.
diagram.root_cause: Cause not published in the retained provider evidence.
diagram.contributors: A backlog was reported during recovery; its presence does not establish what caused the initial failure.
diagram.symptoms: Multiple products were affected and pending work remained during recovery.

steps.label: Requests and queued work progress
steps.detail: Actions and publication workflows depend on completing queued operations as well as accepting new requests.

steps.label: Initial failure not explained
steps.detail: The retained notices do not identify the initiating technical fault or internal dependency.

steps.label: Products degraded; backlog observed
steps.detail: The provider named Actions, Pages and Copilot impacts and subsequently reported recovery with remaining backlog.

steps.label: Backlog processed; incident resolved
steps.detail: A later notice reported backlog processing and resolution. No invented deployment, database repair or traffic cause is added.

relevance.rationale: Directly useful across software and AI systems: Notion's confirmed external classification workflow illustrates how customer text and embedded credentials can cross a processor boundary. The lesson applies beyond this vendor or product. Sources: Notion security advisory; Fireworks AI security bulletins.

detail.rationale: Notion supplies a supported data-flow-to-exposure chain and dated containment/key-response actions; Fireworks distinguishes two contextual intrusion mechanisms. This meets causal-chain-and-response-with-gaps, not a fully demonstrated technical retrospective: the Notion-specific entry vector, authorization/storage path and intrusion mapping remain unpublished. Sources: Notion security advisory; Fireworks AI November 17 bulletin.

transferability.rationale: The evidence supports reusable design tradeoffs between classification utility/debugging and retained text, metadata removal versus content minimization, and data deletion versus issuer revocation. A synthetic-data exercise makes those choices and response boundaries testable without pretending the exact exploit is known. Basis: Notion's confirmed transcript/key exposure and response; Fireworks' bounded vendor mechanisms and rotation advice.

confidence.rationale: The dossier attributes confirmed customer transcripts, embedded-key actions and distinct vendor intrusions to two primary first-party disclosures, with revisions reconciled and limits explicit. This supports the processor-boundary lesson, but not a detailed, independently verified end-to-end forensic account; the second investigation and customer-to-intrusion mapping remain unresolved. Sources: Notion security advisory; Fireworks AI security bulletins. This writer used the supplied source-grounded dossier, not new source fetches.

advisory:notion-fireworks-2026.why: Notion's disclosure supports studying a concrete boundary failure without reconstructing the exploit: removing labels does not remove sensitive text, and removing copies does not invalidate authority carried in that text.
advisory:notion-fireworks-2026.learn: Practice choosing the smallest useful classification input and defining a separate completion criterion for credential recovery. The architecture exercise tests both rather than treating provider disconnection as complete remediation.

diagram.normal: Insights classification crossed an external-processor boundary with chat content. Separately reported open-weight model inference is not the established transcript-exposure path.
diagram.root_cause: Partial supported mechanism: unauthorized vendor-side access exposed customer Insights transcripts. The initial intrusion vector, dataset-access path and mapping to either vendor intrusion are UNKNOWN. No specific failed Notion control is established.
diagram.contributors: Vendor-held customer transcripts created an external content exposure surface; some messages contained API keys. Missing identity labels did not remove embedded secrets. Storage and retention implementation remain unpublished. The vendor's two distinct intrusion paths are contextual evidence, not proven contributors to Notion's specific exposure.
diagram.symptoms: Confirmed transcript exposure affected less than 1% of workspaces and prompted embedded-key response; exact counts and downstream misuse remain unknown. Insights disablement and model-provider removal were containment-related product changes, not proof that every disabled workflow was compromised.

steps.label: Insights crosses processor boundary
steps.detail: Notion describes external classification for Insights. Sending content for that responsibility extends the confidentiality boundary beyond Notion; it does not establish a particular storage design.

steps.label: Vendor dataset contains transcripts
steps.detail: Notion identified customer transcripts in the final impacted dataset. Their presence explains what could be exposed, but not the retention purpose, duration or collection path.

steps.label: UNKNOWN intrusion-to-dataset path
steps.detail: The unauthorized entry vector and authorization crossing that reached Notion's dataset are UNKNOWN. The vendor separately reports an August 3–October 7 stolen-credential/service-vulnerability intrusion and an October 23–30 cloud-development-to-production intrusion. These are contextual paths, not alternative proven explanations for Notion: neither disclosure maps its transcripts to either intrusion or both.

steps.label: Vendor access exposes customer text
steps.detail: Notion confirms transcripts in the accessed dataset despite the preceding gap. Unauthorized access defeats confidentiality because customer content was within the accessed material; retrieval and exfiltration details are unpublished.

steps.label: Text includes credential exposure
steps.detail: Less than 1% of Notion workspaces were affected, and affected user messages contained API keys. Text can therefore carry sensitive material even without author/workspace labels. Credential exposure creates possible downstream access risk, but subsequent use of these keys is not established.

steps.label: Disconnect and remove vendor data
steps.detail: Notion disconnected Fireworks by November 3 and deleted its data there November 4, before final customer dataset confirmation. It also disabled Insights and removed Fireworks-served open-weight models. These containment actions reduced ongoing dependency/exposure; they neither explain the intrusion nor prove recovery of accessed copies. This causal chain does not imply every response waited for customer-data confirmation.

steps.label: Revoke keys and reach issuers
steps.detail: Notion revoked its exposed keys November 11 and contacted third-party issuers November 12. Copy removal cannot revoke authentication authority, so issuer action is a separate recovery track. Third-party revocation outcomes remain unknown.

architecture.invariant: Inferred design question: can Insights obtain useful classifications without leaving reusable customer text or credential material available beyond its necessary processing lifetime? Notion's disclosure establishes the exposure surface, not the intended retention invariant.
architecture.response: Detection: Notion describes vendor notifications and dataset analysis, not the intrusion detector for its transcripts. Containment: disconnection and deletion preceded final scope confirmation. Recovery: Notion-key revocation invalidated those exposed keys; third-party notification is not confirmed revocation, and copied text cannot be recalled. Fireworks reports remediation, with second-intrusion forensics ongoing. The alternatives below are proposed prevention and recovery design, not assertions about missing controls.

decisions.title: Reduce the content that can become a retained dataset
decisions.proposal: Proposed for steps 1 to 2: compare full transcripts with task-specific excerpts or derived classification signals and a bounded deletion lifecycle. Less retained source text reduces the material exposed if the processor boundary is later crossed.
decisions.tradeoff: Narrower inputs can reduce classification accuracy and remove debugging evidence; lifecycle enforcement requires visibility into copies and derived stores.
decisions.residual_risk: Necessary text and processing-time copies remain exposed to compromise. Without service-specific storage evidence, no retention duration or deletion guarantee can be selected.

decisions.title: Keep credential authority out of classification text
decisions.proposal: Proposed for steps 4 to 5: detect and replace credential-shaped content before external classification. This weakens the transition from readable transcript exposure to reusable credential exposure rather than relying on removed author labels.
decisions.tradeoff: False positives discard useful context; false negatives and changing secret formats require evaluation and maintenance.
decisions.residual_risk: Unrecognized keys and identifying prose may survive. Redaction neither prevents vendor compromise nor establishes that Notion lacked filtering.

decisions.title: Track authority recovery separately from copy removal
decisions.proposal: Proposed for steps 6 to 7: maintain issuer ownership and confirmation tracking so deletion does not close the credential-response task. Verify revocation through the issuer or a safe test system, not notification delivery.
decisions.tradeoff: Rotation can disrupt integrations; third-party cooperation and customer coordination can delay closure.
decisions.residual_risk: Revocation blocks future use, not prior misuse; copied content and unidentified credentials remain unresolved.

architecture.validation: Proposed exercise: run synthetic chats with invented identities and fake key markers through full-text, excerpted and redacted classification variants in a controlled test processor. Measure classification agreement, sensitive markers retained and deletion latency. Simulate exposure and disconnect before scope analysis finishes; record that new transfers stop while old copies remain a separate question. Use only a local mock credential issuer to verify that deletion leaves a dummy credential valid until revocation. Choose a design only after measuring utility and obtaining workflow-specific retention, copy inventory and issuer-response evidence.
